newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudan planes bomb northern Uganda, aid workers.
newsitem.headline: Sudan planes bomb northern Uganda, aid workers.

text.p: Sudanese government warplanes bombed a town in northern Uganda on Sunday but there were no immediate reports of casualties, aid workers said on Monday.
The attack dealt a blow to an Iranian-mediated agreement this month to end disputes between Uganda and Sudan which both accuse each other of supporting rebel groups.
"Two Sudanese MiGs came over on Sunday and dropped a number of bombs, around 10. Not all fell on Moyo and we have no reports of casualties," an aid worker, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

Other aid workers said they heard from the region that the MiGs attacked at 9:30 a.m. and dropped bombs and fired rockets at Moyo but no reports of casualties or damage were received, possibly as there were no aid agencies in the immediate area.
The British Broadcasting Corporation said Ugandan authorities had accused Sudan of launching the raid on Moyo town but there was no independent confirmation.
Moyo is about 20 km (12 miles) south of Uganda's border with Sudan. The government in Kampala accused Khartoum of sending warplanes to bomb northern Uganda several times last year.
Sunday's raid was a blow to an agreement earlier this month between Kampala and Khartoum on steps to resolve a long-standing dispute over support for rebels, aid officials said.
Under the September 9 agreement the Ugandan and Sudanese governments agreed to work to halt activity by rebels in the border area.
The two countries agreed to move any refugees and "hostile elements" to at least 100 km (60 miles) from the Uganda-Sudan border, and to encourage voluntary repatriation of refugees.
The main southern Sudanese rebel group, the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), had refused to comment on the pact.

But on Monday SPLA Information Secretary Pa'gan Amum told Reuters: "The raid on Sunday is no surprise in as much as...the agreement is not working and will not work because Khartoum is an expanisionist force and will not abide by any agreement."
He said the SPLA had no presence in Uganda so the raid was apparently a move by Khartoum to act in support of the Ugandan rebel West Nile Bank Front, which is active in the Moyo region.
The leader of the main Sudanese opposition alliance, based in Eritrea, had dismissed the pact mediated by Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on a visit to Khartoum and Kampala as meaningless.
Mubarak al-Mahdi, secretary-general of the National Democratic Alliance, said he had no faith it would work as there was no confidence between the Ugandan and Sudanese governments.
He said he believed Khartoum would keep supplying arms to rebels of the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) fighting in northern Uganda and the SPLA would continue to have good ties to Kampala.
The LRA denies being armed by Khartoum and the SPLA denies being backed by Kampala.
The September 9 pact aimed at stopping the LRA taking refuge in southern Sudan and the SPLA taking refuge in northern Uganda.
Ugandan officials said there was no provision in the agreement for both countries to restore relations but said it included a foreign verification team to monitor the border area.

The SPLA has fought for greater autonomy or the independence of the mainly Christian and animist south from the Moslem, Arabised north since 1983. Uganda broke relations with Sudan in April last year.
